I think this section is misplaced. It should be part of https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/structured-data.html#safe-passing-of-structured-data, probably a new sub-section at the end.

For the dev edition, the contents of this new subsection (not including its heading) should be the only content of the "Safe passing of structured data" section.
@domenic I hope I understood your feedback right. PTAL

As a web developer / JS API user I don't care so much about how the object gets cloned (whether the "structural clone algorithm" is used or a different way of deep cloning). The name of the method doesn't have to reflect the choice of algorithm used by the implementation.

Could the method be called clone() instead of structuredClone() ?  or eg deepClone() or completeClone() or completeCopy() -
or perhaps just simply copy() ? (I haven't gone through all existing names)

> The name of the method doesn't have to reflect the choice of algorithm 

I disagree. The name should to convey what kind of clone the result is. The method `structuredClone` give you a, well, structured clone. Meaning it directly implies what will be cloned and what will not be cloned (e.g. methods and prototypes are _not_ cloned).

A name like `deepClone` or `completeCopy` could set expectations with the developer that are not being fulfilled. That’s how we end up with misnomers on the platform.

I see, thanks for your reply.

Perhaps we do need a method deepClone() or completeCopy()?
Yeah, we have talked about that. But cloning functions is not trivial. Please continue discussing that matter in #793 :)

To reiterate, my main problem with this proposal is that it doesn't expose the full underlying primitive, but rather a subset, and it's unclear how to extend it to expose it fully. The primitive we have is one that takes a value and a transfer list, and returns a value and a transfer list. And the transfer list can be independent from the value. This API just drops the return transfer list on the floor.
Thanks for re-iterating, I didn’t get that before. That’s fair, I guess. I don’t see a problem with changing the returned value to `{cloned, transferredValues}`.

I'm not sure that primitive is terribly important. I think it's more for handling cases where for whatever reason you don't put the transferred values inside the cloned data, and for spec convenience in not making you dig through to find those values, but IMO such cases are not an important part of the primitive...

I agree, but I’m also not sure if we are thinking of everything that could be needed in the future. I’ll leave that decision up to you all, I don’t have very strong feelings either way, although in terms of developer ergonomics and arguably the current 99% use-case, returning just the clone seems more desirable.

FWIW, +1 for just returning the deserialized values. It'd be really easy for a caller to get if they wanted, be serializing `{data, transferList}` themselves. Currently [[TransferredValues]] is only exposed insofar as MessagePort objects are extracted from there and separately exposed. As a result, Blink doesn't actually keep the original transfer list in order at present (we have separate lists for ports, buffers, etc.).
The original PR for tests got side-tracked and the actual PR for adding tests for `structuredClone()` now lives in w3c/web-platform-tests#11069.

Just wondering: I am not sure what the result of the conversation so far is. Have we reached some sort of consensus weather `transferList` should be exposed by `structuredClone()`? What are we missing to qualify for “implementer interest”?

I don't know about consensus, but I feel it should definitely be there, and my read of @annevk was that he didn't feel _too_ strongly against it...

What we're missing in terms of implementer interest is outlined in https://whatwg.org/working-mode#additions. So far I don't see any browser engineers saying "we would like to implement this soon" on this thread.
I suspect Firefox would adopt this pretty quickly, but it'd be good if someone could go over https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/793#issuecomment-389192421 and work through @wanderview's concern.

Can you guys have a look once at https://github.com/tc39/proposals/issues/150

Can we guys discuss?
It is sad that there is not more interest shown, considering that the top 3 npm packages for cloning have over 100k weekly downloads
Is there any status on this? Was it ever implemented in any browsers, e.g. Chrome? I can't find anything similar in my JS console in the latest Chrome.

The status remains as of https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3414#issuecomment-390714274. Per @annevk's comment it sounds like Firefox is interested in implementing, but perhaps not being the first to implement. Sadly, nobody else is, including Chrome (despite a Chrome engineer proposing this).

While I am not sure it was ever contentious, I wanted to make sure that this kind of function is actually in high demand and would be a useful addition to the platform á la Extensible Web Manifesto.


I ran an [HTTPArchive](https://httparchive.org/) query to figure out how often deep cloning is used on the most popular sites.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT page from httparchive.response_bodies.2020_03_01_mobile WHERE UPPER(body) LIKE '%CLONEDEEP%';
```

**425,170 of 5,960,921 HAR-crawled pages (~7%) seem to use lodash’s deep cloning implementation.** 


Caveats: 

1. This is only evaluating landing URLs of popular websites.
2. It’s a string match, which could very-well be a false positive. 
3. Just because it’s shipped doesn’t mean it’s used. 
4. The string that is matched is the function name that the arguably most popular library uses: [`cloneDeep`](https://github.com/lodash/lodash/blob/ddfd9b11a0126db2302cb70ec9973b66baec0975/lodash.js#L11087). There might be deep clone implementations with other (or obfuscated) names.

Libraries would be an obvious customer for this function.

I had a brief chat with @bakulf about returning a "clone" versus returning a promise for a "clone" and while our current implementation is fully synchronous, it is a heavy operation and being able to optimize it and make it partially non-blocking going forward might be good.

On the other hand, the libraries @surma found use a synchronous version which means they would have a harder transition path.

But yeah, the main thing needed here would be @mfreed7 or @cdumez or some such +1'ing the whole thing on behalf of Chromium/WebKit.
I mean we have tons of code floating around using synchronous `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` but that's not necessarily a good reason not to buck the trend

> I had a brief chat with @bakulf about returning a "clone" versus returning a promise for a "clone" and while our current implementation is fully synchronous, it is a heavy operation and being able to optimize it and make it partially non-blocking going forward might be good.

Pretty much all code in the wild currently synchronous for a deep-copy, and I believe this would be strictly faster (albeit synchronous). It wouldn’t cause a performance regression as far as I can tell.

That being said, I find the idea of an (additional) asynchronous structured clone appealing. Thinking about it a bit more, I guess only the _deserialze_ part of structured cloning can be done asynchronously?    Making the _serialize_ part synchronous seems problematic if the value-to-be-cloned is mutated during the serialize. (Should we move the asynchronous structured clone disussion to a separate issue?)
I don't think we should have both APIs.
I think exposing the sync API should be higher priority, since otherwise people would have to continue using terrible workarounds with `history.state` to get the same effect.
To be clear, that API uses StructuredSerializeForStorage and we've talked about imposing an upper limit for that variant so I don't think it's directly comparable nor necessarily a suitable polyfill.

> Making the serialize part synchronous seems problematic if the value-to-be-cloned is mutated during the serialize.

Mutation of the input (graph) is a specific case of the broader problem: the operation has an unknown number of side-effects which can be observed from ES. I think an async API for serialization should be considered a non-starter for the reasons described in [Design Principles / Preserve run-to-completion semantics](https://w3ctag.github.io/design-principles/#js-rtc) — it’s a lot of recursive Gets and GetPrototypeOfs etc, not work the agent does unobservably “in the background”.

This would be incredibly useful. Having an 'overridable' method (under a well-known Symbol perhaps - `Symbol.copy/clone/etc`) would allow the necessary polymorphic hooks to allow the level of customization that we see out here in the wild.

We discussed this feature in the triage call and there's mild interest in exposing this functionality in browsers. One thing that would really help move that along is getting a better understanding of the use cases people have for this. We know that this is somewhat popular, but it's not entirely clear why it is popular, if that makes sense. 😊

So if folks could summarize how and why they might use this, that would really help! Thanks.
@annevk A native deepClone would help developers newer to js avoid picking non-ideal implementations in userland libraries (saw this happen twice training new devs over the last 9 years)
Native deep clone? I vote yes!!! 😄

My use case: I am creating a polyfill for a new browser standard, and that standard is using Structured Clone to provide a copy of some data to consumers of that standard. However, my polyfill can't use that, and instead the closest I can get (without pulling in a large 3rd party library) is just the standard JSON.stringify + JSON.parse trick. However, that has its own shortcomings and isn't as comprehensive as Structured Clone is; so my polyfill will have some shortcomings/discrepancies  compared to what browsers will provide.

My use case: as an author of API libraries I want to be able to transform user-passed data without worrying about affecting the originating input. I have written deep copy shims many many times and having it supported at the platform level would be very helpful.

This would be so handy! Here are a few of the cloneDeep use cases I run into often:

1. I need to park a canonical copy of a data structure that will be fed to code that may mutate it in ways I don't control. E.g. I have set up a complicated config+data object and fed it to a charting library which mutates the data structure internally in response to user interaction; separately, a settings widget is powered by the same config object, but will be flummoxed by the mutations.
2. I need to park a canonical copy of a data structure so I can implement a "revert changes" workflow without setting up a whole undo/redo stack.
3. Copy/paste implementations.

Also +1 for an option to do this asynchronously -- in examples 1 & 2 above, we would generally perform a deep clone in the data-fetching layer of our program, before passing both a sealed and an unsealed copy back to other modules, so we're already running in an asynchronous context. Although I agree that a synchronous method is likely to be more widely applicable / more of a priority.

Main use cases for this I have seen in our code seem to be around copying default value objects to initialize new model data, or copying model data for immutability purposes.

We have some related cases for copying data structures for delayed logging, but these also need to address circular references so probably are not strictly related to the structuredClone algorithm as we want to break any circular references to create clean serialized forms. Though we may be interested in using structuredClone for this and then breaking the references at serialization time instead.

This is not an argument against `structuredClone()` at all, which does seem useful in its own right, but sharing a minor data point about how it surprised me what "exposing structured clone" ended up meaning here:

Each time I've had to implement ersatz structured clone - usually in the context of polyfilling platform features - what I needed was `serialize(x)` and `deserialize(y)`. Since `structuredClone()` seems to be an all-in-one `deserialize(serialize(x))`, it doesn't seem to help with cases that need, specifically, "the structured clone API" - only cases that need "a convenient clone function".

Using functional programming practices can make the code more correct. This requires using immutable value objects which are copied before they are modified, helping us achieve referential transparency. Structured cloning will allow us to do the copying in a more efficient way.

Two use cases I have:
* Forking and editing an object which can be diffed against the original.
* Suppose I'm building a library and I want to expose some internal state. I want the caller to be able to mutate the returned state but I don't want their mutations to leak into the internal state of the library.

There are alternative approaches to cloning for both of the above but having a fast primitive could be very useful. Notably, `Object.freeze`.
I personally don't see how transferables make any sense since all the use cases are for cloning data in the same context.

> I personally don't see how transferables make any sense 

It’s certainly niche. I expect that most usages of `structuredClone()` would ignore that parameter. It’s exposed for completeness sake, as it is part of the structured clone algorithm. I think this can be important, for example fore polyfill authoring.
Yes. In general I don’t think there is a synchronous way to neuter an ArrayBuffer.
@surma can you grant write access to `surma-dump/html` so we can push minor changes and help with rebasing?

Expanding on the last few comments, I forgot that I myself have had a use case for this as a library author: see the explanation in https://github.com/domenic/proposal-arraybuffer-transfer#the-problem . Although that explanation is ArrayBuffer-specific, as is the proposed solution there, in fact the use case occurs with more than just ArrayBuffers, and so a more general solution like `self.structuredClone()` that works for all transferables (including, e.g., ImageBitmaps or web codecs stuff) would be better IMO.
@bathos I tend to agree it might be worth solving that, but it's a lot more involved. #3517 should probably be used to track that idea.
